The problem requires computing $I = \int_{-9}^{11} f(x) \, dx$, where $f(x^7 + 6x^5 + 3x^3 + 1) = 9x + 5$.

Let $p(x) = x^7 + 6x^5 + 3x^3 + 1$. We are given $f(p(x)) = 9x + 5$.
The limits of integration, $x=-9$ and $x=11$, correspond to $p(-1) = -9$ and $p(1) = 11$.
Using the substitution $x = p(t)$, we have $dx = p'(t) dt$.
$$
I = \int_{p(-1)}^{p(1)} f(x) \, dx = \int_{-1}^{1} f(p(t)) p'(t) dt
$$
Since $f(p(t)) = 9t + 5$ and $p'(t) = 7t^6 + 30t^4 + 9t^2$:
$$
I = \int_{-1}^{1} (9t + 5) (7t^6 + 30t^4 + 9t^2) dt
$$
$$
I = 9 \int_{-1}^{1} t (7t^6 + 30t^4 + 9t^2) dt + 5 \int_{-1}^{1} (7t^6 + 30t^4 + 9t^2) dt
$$
The first term is the integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval, so it is 0.
The second term uses the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus:
$$
5 \int_{-1}^{1} p'(t) dt = 5 [p(1) - p(-1)] = 5 [11 - (-9)] = 5(20) = 100.
$$
The correct value is $I = 100$.

Solution 3 yields $10$. It ignores the Jacobian $p'(t)$, assuming $p'(t)=1$.
